summaries.Q3329089: In 1885 the Clermont industrialist Jean-Baptiste Bargoin left part of his fortune to the city to found a museum; the building, by Joseph Dionnet, opened in 1903. Intended for the fine arts, the museum showed archaeological pieces from the start. In the basement, 10,000 fragments of wooden ex-votos from the source des Roches, in Chamalières.
summaries.Q1495869: An Ursuline convent until the Revolution, the buildings served as barracks, a major seminary, a military hospital, then a gendarmerie until 1982. Adrien Fainsilber and Clermont-born Claude Gaillard fitted out a museum, opened in 1992 around a central atrium under a glass roof. In 1999 it took the name of Roger Quilliot, former mayor and minister.
summaries.Q3330860: The naturalist Henri Lecoq left his collections to Clermont-Ferrand, which bought his town house to turn it into a natural history museum, opened in 1873. Over 200,000 plants, 300,000 animals including 200,000 insects: among them Aphodius arvernicus, a beetle held to be endemic to Auvergne, proved to be a scientific hoax.
summaries.Q56827114: A museum devoted to the Michelin group, opened on 23 January 2009, it retraces over 2,000 m2 the group's history, heritage and industrial products. On show are the 1895 car L'Éclair, a Breguet 14 aircraft from the First World War and a Micheline railcar. The museum drew 100,000 visitors in 2019.
summaries.Q85821952: Born of the revolutionary confiscations of 1791, which gathered the books of the cathedral chapter and of the city's convents, the library opened to the public in 1800 and moved to rue Bardoux in 1994. It holds 7 kilometres of documents, including the Breviary of Alaric, whose margin bears Tomida femina, one of the oldest Occitan texts.
summaries.Q770459: The name of this Romanesque collegiate church is said to come from the Port district, from the Latin portus, “the warehouse”, the place where goods were stored. Built in pale arkose from the 1120s-1130s, it was nearly razed in 1800 for a cloth market and was saved by a petition. Leo XIII raised it to minor basilica in 1881.
summaries.Q3580231: As a charter of 1196 barred clerics from living in Montferrand, the churches were built outside the walls; only the castle chapel was allowed within. The Hundred Years' War led the inhabitants to obtain a parish inside the walls, set up in this castle chapel and turned from 1340 into a church of southern Gothic style.
summaries.Q22928172: Settled in Clermont in 1288, the Carmelites finished the choir and bell tower of their church in 1371; it was consecrated in 1472. The Revolution destroyed it: only the Carmelite chapel stood, given to the town, then to the Protestants, then to a cooper as his workshop. Returned to worship, it took the name Saint-Genès-des-Carmes in 1802.
summaries.Q22928176: The church of Saint-Laurent stands in Clermont-Ferrand, in the Puy-de-Dôme. It has been listed as a monument historique since 31 December 1976.
summaries.Q3581416: This former collegiate church in neo-Gothic style was built between 1858 and 1862, in place of a medieval building probably dating from the 12th century and demolished in 1858. Registered as a monument historique since 1986, it underwent a major restoration completed in 2015.
summaries.Q3583584: Built in the 17th century for the Minim convent, this classical-style church has its east entrance on the place de Jaude. Jean Teillard enlarged it in the 19th century; the sculptures inside are by Henri Gourgouillon. It has been registered as a monument historique since 1987.
summaries.Q2957289: Hugues Imbert drew the plans of this neoclassical chapel under one constraint: separate access for the residents, the congregation and the public. Completed between 1850 and 1855, it has a Greek-cross plan, each arm with its own entrance. The hospital was pulled down in the 1980s; only the chapel survived, reopened in 2010 as an exhibition space.
summaries.Q3354572: Built from 1891 to 1894 under Jean Teillard, on the site of the Halle aux toiles, it replaced the theatre on the place Royale, judged too small. After part of the ceiling collapsed it stayed shut for seven years and reopened on 20 September 2013; the works uncovered Louis Retru's frescoes behind the hangings of the foyer.
summaries.Q2996610: The concert hall stands on the site of the former Michelin cooperative, a department store for the workers, and opened on 7 March 2000 with Les Rita Mitsouko. Labelled a scène de musiques actuelles, it puts on about 130 concerts a year between its 460-seat Club and its Grande Salle of 1,500.
summaries.Q15950424: Émile Camut built this town house in 1897 for Joseph Cote, a businessman who became Cote-Blatin after marrying Antoinette Blatin. In Volvic stone, it stands out for its slate roof, in contrast with the tiles and flat roofs of the neighbourhood. The 2010 registration covers the interior decoration and the garden.
summaries.Q22928279: The stair turret, built in the late 15th or early 16th century, bears the high relief that gives the house its name: on the balustrade, a snake with a human head coils around the apple tree, which Adam and Eve point at. Of the early 13th-century main block, demolished before the 1924 listing, only the street front remains.
summaries.Q15950584: Begun in the 1760s by Pierre Peyrat, this Louis XVI hôtel opens onto an oval courtyard of honour. Sold as national property during the Revolution, it was recovered by Antoine de Chazerat in 1806, then housed the bishopric, a hospital during the First World War and the arts faculty until 1937. The DRAC moved in in 1982.
summaries.Q3145837: Gabriel de Fontfreyde, a Clermont merchant, bought this house in the 16th century and rebuilt it, having his arms carved on the keystone of the shop arch. The Doric, Ionic and Corinthian orders set one above the other on the courtyard betray the influence of architectural treatises, hence its nickname “maison des architectes”.
summaries.Q22928308: Built in the late 12th or early 13th century, the hôtel de la Chanterie is one of the oldest buildings in the medieval centre of Montferrand and owes its name to the Grand Chantre, who probably lived there. Its Romanesque arcades, no doubt shops, suggest a wealthy merchant; heavy grilles recall a past use as a prison.
summaries.Q111482612: Blaise Pascal stayed twice at this château of his brother-in-law Florin Périer, where in 1664 his sister Gilberte took the manuscripts of the Pensées, kept for fifty years. A rubber maker set up in the former library: in 1856 the benzene caught fire and burned the building down. Michelin razed it in 1914 for the Carmes factory.
summaries.Q22997576: Raised from the last quarter of the 12th century to the 16th century to protect the counts' town, the Montferrand wall had 1,773 metres of curtain, twenty-two towers and four gates; about 900 metres and thirteen towers survive. In 1388 Perrot le Béarnais got into the town by hiding his men in barrels.
summaries.Q3146105: In 1910 prefect Becq warned the departmental council: in twenty years fifteen employees had died from the unhealthy premises. A competition open only to architects of the department was won in 1913 by François Clermont; work began in May 1914. Alexandre Millerand inaugurated the building on 7 July 1923.
summaries.Q2871713: The name of this Gallo-Roman town means “sanctuary of Augustus”. Its forum crowned the hill where the cathedral and the place de la Victoire stand. In the 2nd century it had 15,000 to 30,000 inhabitants, one of the most populous in Roman Gaul; withdrawn behind its walls, it held only about 700 from the 4th century.
summaries.Q3123055: Finished in 1844 in the workshop of Charles-François Lebœuf, known as Nanteuil, the statue of the general who died at Marengo was unveiled on 13 August 1848, still on a temporary pedestal of brick and wood, before his former comrades in arms. The present base dates from 1903, the year Bartholdi's Vercingetorix opposite was unveiled.
summaries.Q3076110: Jacques d'Amboise, bishop of Clermont, had it made from 1511 by the sculptor Chapart, in Volvic stone: the architecture is still Gothic, the carved decoration already Renaissance. First set before the south portal of the cathedral, it has been moved four times and has stood on the place Olympe-de-Gouges since 1962.
summaries.Q15948808: Built in 1875, this fountain stands on the central island of the place Delille. It has been registered as a monument historique since 2007.
summaries.Q15113638: This 18th-century fountain in Volvic stone stands on the boulevard Trudaine, on the small square formed where the rue des Archers comes out. It owes its name to the guild of the chevaliers de la Flèche, whose seat stood close by, cour des Archers. The water flows from the mouths of two carved masks.
summaries.Q15948828: Built in 1602, it stands in the middle of the place du Terrail, in the historic centre, east of the cathedral. It has been registered as a monument historique since 1987.
summaries.Q3076238: Built in 1858 on the place de la Rodade, in the western part of the Montferrand district, this Volvic stone fountain carries on each face of its shaft one of the four seasons, among horns of plenty, scrollwork and mascarons. It watered the animals of the fairground. Its gas lantern has been replaced by a modern one.
summaries.Q1152655: This five-hectare park descends from the botanical garden created in 1781, which Henri Lecoq took charge of in 1821; it received its name in 1871. In 1862 the landscape designer Choulot proposed a new plan, carried out by the engineer Guyot under Lecoq. In 1915 the porch and turret of the château de Bien-Assis were re-erected there.
summaries.Q3390247: The best-known square in Clermont-Ferrand occupies the eastern part of the Jaude maar, a phreatomagmatic volcano 1.5 km across to which it gave its name. Bartholdi's equestrian Vercingetorix was unveiled here in 1903. The north forecourt, in dark basalt, is lit at night by 250 red and yellow diodes figuring the movement of lava.
summaries.Q16670270: It is commonly held that Pope Urban II preached the First Crusade here, in 1095, but no chronicler recorded the exact place: the square is only a plausible hypothesis. It owes its name to the abbé Delille, a Clermont poet, and its fountain, made around 1875, has been listed with its underground network since 2007.
summaries.Q3390462: The cathedral forecourt covers the forum of Augustonemetum; it was cleared only after the Revolution, by the destruction of the bishop's palace and the medieval quarter. The fountain with the statue of Urban II dates from 1898. In 2024 the Christmas market moved to place de Jaude: heavy trucks risked weakening the cellars and tunnels.
summaries.Q28040721: In old Montferrand, this street once called de l'Hôpital and de la Fontaine links the carrefour des Taules to the place de la Fontaine. Town houses follow one another: at no. 11 the hôtel d'Albiat, or Maison des Centaures; at no. 28 the hôtel Fontfreyde, or Maison de Lucrèce. No. 16 holds a 14th-century wall painting, a Saint Christopher.
summaries.Q16533596: Cut on the line of the town ditches by the intendant Ballainvilliers, it was called boulevard du Grand-Séminaire before taking in 1880 the name of the Clermont administrator Trudaine de Montigny. Its two sides are unalike: to the west, bars and restaurants follow one another; to the east, not a shop, nor even a street opening onto it.
summaries.Q60846407: At the gates of the medieval town of Montferrand, the square took shape outside the walls, on the ditches: the south gate opened at the crossing with rue Jules-Guesde. The fountain that gives it its name stood at its centre from the 19th century; it was moved in 2005 for the tramway line, which cuts the square in two.
summaries.Q3322688: Founded ex nihilo at the turn of the 12th century by the counts of Auvergne facing Clermont, the bishops' city, Montferrand received the oldest charter of franchises in the region and governed itself until 1731, when the 1630 edict of Troyes was at last applied. It would ask for separation in 1789, 1848, 1863 and 1911.
summaries.Q15952731: This covered market was built in 1891-1892. It has been registered as a monument historique since 2002.
summaries.Q2944824: Judged unsanitary, the Fond de Jaude district was razed to make way for this shopping centre: the shops opened on 11 September 1980. Jean-Loup Roubert designed it in concrete, with passages “in the tradition of the covered arcades of the 19th century”. In 2008 the white tiling of its façades on the square vanished under 1,600 m² of glass.
summaries.Q42168: The historic capital of Auvergne, the city was born in the 17th century from the union of two rival towns, Clermont and Montferrand. Home of Michelin, it has more than 40,000 students, a quarter of its population. It spreads at the foot of the Limagne fault and the Chaîne des Puys, on the UNESCO World Heritage list since 2018.
summaries.Q1164900: Michelin funded the building of this rugby ground in 1911, on the initiative of its manager Marcel Michelin, who died in deportation. The ground belongs to ASM Clermont Auvergne but stands on land leased from the Manufacture des Pneus. A stand bears the name of Jean-François Phliponeau, a Montferrand player who collapsed on the pitch on 8 May 1976.
summaries.Q3268594: Founded in 1576, the former Jesuit college changed status several times: Institut in 1791, école centrale in 1796, lycée impérial in 1808, collège royal in 1815, lycée impérial again in 1853, before becoming lycée Blaise-Pascal in 1871. The new buildings, begun in 1954 on the grounds of the Gribeauval barracks, opened in 1956.
summaries.Q2972588: The city's oldest working cemetery occupies the grounds of the former abbey of the Discalced Carmelites, bought in January 1816 by the city and the diocese for 36,000 francs. Eleven hectares cut in two by the Tiretaine, where almost every tomb built up to the mid-1940s is of dark grey Volvic stone.
summaries.Q1032205: Struck by the Sainte-Chapelle, bishop Hugues de la Tour began the works in 1248. This was the first use of Volvic stone in architecture: dark, strong enough to allow very slender piers, it earned the building the nickname “cathedral of the coalmen” from the Goncourts. The west front was only completed in 1884.
summaries.Q2820668: This Benedictine abbey, founded beside the tomb of Saint Alyre, remained independent of the bishop of Clermont until 1374. A prison during the Revolution, sold in 1791 then largely destroyed, it became a boarding school in 1796, then barracks; the Ursulines moved in in 1807. The buildings now house the Institution Saint-Alyre.
summaries.Q15958101: This chapel on the avenue d'Italie, fitted out in the former Vox cinema, holds Mass in the Tridentine rite. It grew out of the mission led in the Puy-de-Dôme in 1976 by Father Paul Aulagnier, sent by Archbishop Lefebvre, with lay people attached to the old Mass. Priests of the Society of Saint Pius X conduct the services.
summaries.Q15945291: The chapel is said to have been founded by the Franciscans in 1273, on land given ten years earlier by Bernard de la Tour, whose family was later buried there. Sold as national property during the Revolution, the Cordeliers convent vanished through successive demolitions: only the chapel remains, now part of the departmental council seat.
summaries.Q3497631: Bartholdi first designed this equestrian statue for the Gergovie plateau, but its size ruled that out; scaled down, it was raised on the place de Jaude and unveiled in October 1903. The horse leaps over a fallen Roman, no hoof touching the ground, and the face of the Arverni chief is modelled on that of a young Napoleon III.
summaries.Q15948823: General Desaix, a local son, died at Marengo on 14 June 1800, aged 31; the city at once decided on a monument to his glory. The architect Pierre Laurent proposed a fountain centred on an obelisk, recalling the Egyptian campaign; its execution in Volvic stone fell to the sculptor Joseph Chinard, work starting in 1801.
